Sheriffs
shĕr´ĭfs
n. pl. (a class of Babylonian provincial officials)
An English word of Saxon origin — shire-reeve, the king's officer in a county — used by the translators to render an Aramaic term for a class of magistrates. It occurs twice, both in the summons to Nebuchadnezzar's image.

Biblical Definition

Nebuchadnezzar summons the entire administrative apparatus of an empire to one ceremony: “Then Nebuchadnezzar the king sent to gather together the princes, the governors, and the captains, the judges, the treasurers, the counsellors, the sheriffs, and all the rulers of the provinces, to come to the dedication of the image which Nebuchadnezzar the king had set up” (Daniel 3:2). The list is then repeated verbatim as they arrive: “Then the princes, the governors, and captains, the judges, the treasurers, the counsellors, the sheriffs, and all the rulers of the provinces, were gathered together unto the dedication of the image that Nebuchadnezzar the king had set up; and they stood before the image” (Daniel 3:3). The repetition is deliberate and heavy; seven ranks of officialdom, named twice, standing in a plain. The command is total: “That at what time ye hear the sound of the cornet, flute, harp, sackbut, psaltery, dulcimer, and all kinds of musick, ye fall down and worship the golden image” (Daniel 3:5). Against the whole weight of it stand three men with one sentence: “But if not, be it known unto thee, O king, that we will not serve thy gods, nor worship the golden image which thou hast set up” (Daniel 3:18).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines sheriff as an officer in each county to whom is entrusted the execution of the laws; the translators use it for a Chaldean magistrate.

expand to see more

SHERIFF, n. An officer in each county, to whom is entrusted the execution of the laws; from shire and reeve.

MAGISTRATE, n. A public civil officer, invested with the executive government or some branch of it.

PROVINCE, n. A country belonging to a kingdom or state, either by conquest or colonization.

DEDICATION, n. The act of consecrating to a divine Being, or to a sacred use.

CONSCIENCE, n. Internal or self-knowledge; the faculty by which we judge of the moral rectitude of our own actions.

Key Scripture

Daniel 3:2 — "Then Nebuchadnezzar the king sent to gather together the princes, the governors, and the captains, the judges, the treasurers, the counsellors, the sheriffs, and all the rulers of the provinces, to come to the dedication of the image which Nebuchadnezzar the king had set up."

Daniel 3:3 — "Then the princes, the governors, and captains, the judges, the treasurers, the counsellors, the sheriffs, and all the rulers of the provinces, were gathered together unto the dedication of the image that Nebuchadnezzar the king had set up; and they stood before the image that Nebuchadnezzar had set up."

Daniel 3:5 — "That at what time ye hear the sound of the cornet, flute, harp , sackbut, psaltery, dulcimer, and all kinds of musick, ye fall down and worship the golden image that Nebuchadnezzar the king hath set up:"

Daniel 3:18 — "But if not, be it known unto thee, O king, that we will not serve thy gods, nor worship the golden image which thou hast set up."

Modern Corruption

Conscience is treated as a private preference the state may override for the common good, when Daniel 3 sets the whole machinery of an empire against three men and vindicates the three.

expand to see more

Daniel 3 is built to make the reader feel the asymmetry. Seven grades of official are listed twice, six instruments are named, the furnace is heated seven times, and the king asks the question every persecutor asks: who is that God that shall deliver you out of my hands? The answer the three give is the high-water mark of creaturely faith in the Old Testament, and its strength lies in the middle clause. They say God is able to deliver them; they say He will deliver them; and then they say but if not, we will not serve thy gods. Their obedience was not contingent on the outcome.

The doctrine is the limit of the civil magistrate. Scripture commands submission to governing authorities as ordained of God, and the same Scripture records Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego refusing an imperial decree, the apostles answering the Sanhedrin that we ought to obey God rather than men, and the midwives of Egypt lying to Pharaoh and being blessed for it. The magistrate's sphere is real and God-given; it does not extend to the conscience, and where it commands what God forbids or forbids what God commands it must be disobeyed and the penalty accepted. That is the classical Reformed position, and it is why the sheriffs are in the list: to show the reader exactly how much was standing on the other side.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Aramaic tiphtaye (H8614), sheriffs or magistrates; adargazraya (H148), counsellors; tselem (H6755), an image; segan (H5460), a governor.

expand to see more

Aramaic tiphtaye (H8614) — lawyers, magistrates; rendered sheriffs in Daniel 3:2-3.

Aramaic achashdarpenayya (H324) — satraps, the princes of the provinces.

Aramaic segan (H5460) — a prefect, governor; second in the list.

Aramaic tselem (H6755) — an image; the golden image set up in the plain of Dura.

Aramaic segid (H5457) — to prostrate oneself, worship; the act commanded.

Usage

"“The counsellors, the sheriffs, and all the rulers of the provinces” — the summons."

"“They stood before the image” — the same list, arrived."

"“But if not…we will not serve thy gods” — three men against all of it."
